title: Acids and bases
note: Lower pKa means a stronger acid, and each pKa unit is a factor of 10. An acid–base equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid (higher pKa). Anything that stabilizes the conjugate base makes the acid stronger: charge on a more electronegative or larger atom, resonance, nearby electron-withdrawing groups, and more s character.

read.title: Reading a pKa table
text: Organic chemists compare acids with pKa, the negative logarithm of the acid dissociation constant. A small pKa means a strong acid. Because the scale is logarithmic, an acid with pKa 4 is a hundred times stronger than one with pKa 6.

A handful of values covers most problems: HCl about −7, hydronium about −1.7, carboxylic acids about 4 to 5, phenol about 10, alcohols about 16 to 18, ketone α-hydrogens about 19 to 20, terminal alkynes about 25, ammonia about 36 to 38, and alkanes about 50.

To predict whether a reaction happens, find the acid on each side. The equilibrium favors the side with the weaker acid, the one with the higher pKa. Sodium amide removes the proton of a terminal alkyne because the ammonia formed (pKa ~36) is a much weaker acid than the alkyne (pKa ~25). Hydroxide cannot do this job well, because the water it would form is a stronger acid than the alkyne.

The pattern behind the numbers is the stability of the conjugate base. Acetate is stabilized by resonance, so acetic acid is far more acidic than ethanol. Electron-withdrawing fluorines make trifluoroacetic acid stronger still. A lone pair in an sp orbital is held close to carbon, which is why ethyne is so much more acidic than ethane.
